# Tulving & Thomson (1973): Encoding Specificity Principle

## Core Principle

The encoding specificity principle, proposed by Endel Tulving and Donald M. Thomson (1973), states that **when people encode information, they do so in specific ways**, and a retrieval cue will be effective to the extent that it matches or overlaps the memory trace (engram) of the original experience [1][2][3]. Formally, it is defined as "the hypothesis that a retrieval cue will be effective to the extent that information encoded from the cue overlaps or matches information in the engram or memory trace" [2][5]. Whether a cue works depends on how the information was originally encoded [1][2][3].

## The Original 1973 Paper

The paper, *"Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory"* (Psychological Review, 80(5), 352–373), examined retrieval processes and evaluated early theories of retrieval, particularly the generation-recognition theory [4][6]. Experiments testing this theory produced results incompatible with generation-recognition models and most other theories: **under certain conditions, subjects consistently failed to recognize many recallable list words** [4]. This "recognition failure" phenomenon was subsumed under the encoding specificity principle, according to which "the memory trace of an event and hence the properties of effective retrieval cue are determined by the specific encoding operations performed by the system on the input stimuli" [4].

## The Recognition Failure of Recallable Words

A key insight from this work is that recognition tests do not provide perfect indexes of what is stored in memory — people can fail to recognize a target yet later recall it with different cues (Watkins & Tulving, 1975) [1][2][3]. The classic example involves famous authors' surnames: people might fail to recognize "Shaw" as a famous author's name, yet a cued-recall cue like "George Bernard ___" successfully produces "Shaw" [1][2][3]. This is because "George Bernard" matches the way the writer is stored in memory better than the surname itself does — even though the surname is the target [1][2][3]. This demonstrates that the best cues are those that recreate the event or name to be remembered; sometimes even the target itself is not the best cue [1][2][3].

## Supporting Evidence and Related Principles

- **Context effects**: In a classic experiment (Godden & Baddeley, 1975), participants who were tested in the same location where they learned words recalled more than those tested in a new setting — the physical context itself served as a retrieval cue [1][2][3].
- **Cue overload principle**: For a cue to be effective, it cannot match too many other experiences (Watkins, 1975; Nairne, 2002). For example, "William" is a poor cue for recalling Shakespeare because it is overloaded (Prince William, William Yeats, William Faulkner, etc.), whereas "George Bernard ___" is distinctive [1][2][3].
- **Follow-up research**: Salzberg & Pellegrino (1974) replicated the encoding specificity effect in the Tulving-Thomson generation-recognition-recall paradigm, showing the effect in both recognition of generated items and cued recall [7]. De Vito (1975) found that word concreteness differentially affected recognition-cued recall differences for word pairs in a variant of the Tulving-Thomson paradigm [8].

## Practical Implication

Because retrieval is aided by matching the encoding context, the principle explains why studying in the same room where an exam will be taken can improve performance — the physical context provides retrieval cues [1][2][3].

## Summary: Smith (1979, 1985, 1988) on Environmental Context, Recall, Recognition, and the Room-Change Paradigm

Steven M. Smith's research across these three publications examined **environmental context-dependent memory (CDM)** using the **room-change paradigm**, in which participants study material in one room and are tested either in the same room (same context, SC) or a different room (different context, DC), with context reinstatement versus change manipulated between study and test. His work is central to the well-known **dissociation between recall and recognition** under environmental context manipulations.

### Smith (1979): "Remembering In and Out of Context"
In three experiments with 120 college students, Smith established the **environmental reinstatement effect**: subjects remember more when tested in their original learning environment than in a new one.

- **Experiment 1** used an ABA/ABB/ACB design to disentangle context *matching* from context *familiarity*. Group ABA (studied and tested in the same room) recalled significantly more words (24.0) than Group ABB (18.5) or Group ACB (17.7), while the two different-context groups did not differ. This showed the effect is due to a **memory process** (contextual associations), not a general performance decrement caused by the unfamiliarity of the new test room.
- **Experiment 2** found the reinstatement effect was **eliminated** when DC subjects were instructed to recall (internally reinstate) the original learning environment just before free recall—internal reinstatement was as effective as external reinstatement, and instructions to imagine the study room worked as well as showing pictures of it.
- **Experiment 3** showed this "release from contextual dependence" was **diminished when the original learning room was made more difficult to remember** (e.g., when participants encountered five contexts versus only two on day one, they could no longer easily internally reinstate the encoding room). This demonstrated that context effects are under **cognitive control**—subjects can supply their own contextual retrieval cues when the context can be easily recalled.

### Smith (1985): "Environmental Context and Recognition Memory Reconsidered"
This paper challenged the prevailing belief that environmental context affects recall but **not recognition**, by demonstrating that EC-dependent memory *can* occur with recognition memory under certain conditions.

- **Experiment 1**: Five lists were studied, each in a different room, and recognition for all five lists was tested in one of the five rooms. On a yes–no recognition test, recognition was **reliably affected by EC** (context scores significantly greater than zero; mean context score = .02, small but reliable—the first reported finding of EC-dependent recognition).
- **Experiment 2**: Two lists were studied in different rooms and tested in one room using free recall, cued recall, or recognition. Reliable effects of the test room were found **only on the recognition test** (which contained a randomized mix of the two lists). The recognition effect was small (a 2% difference) compared to the 10–25% differences typical in free-recall CDM studies; the greatly reduced error variance from the **within-subjects** SC vs. DC comparison was essential for detecting such small effects. (Free recall failed to show CDM here, likely due to output interference from the recency effect.)
- Field dependence/independence results were inconclusive.

### Smith (1988): "Environmental Context-Dependent Memory" (Review)
This review summarized the state of the field and articulated the **recall–recognition dissociation** and its explanation. While **strong and stable effects of environmental context reinstatement/change have been observed for recall, effects on recognition rarely occur because the word itself is a powerful cue**—the **"outshining hypothesis."** On a recognition test, the test item itself provides a highly specific retrieval cue that "outshines" the weaker environmental context cues, eliminating the advantage of context reinstatement. The review also presented a classification of context effects and specified conditions under which context-dependent effects are likely to be maximized or minimized.

### The Recall–Recognition Dissociation Across Smith's Work
Taken together, these three publications trace a coherent arc: (1) robust, replicable environmental reinstatement effects in **free recall** (1979), with the mechanism being memory-based contextual associations that can be internally reinstated; (2) the demonstration that **recognition memory can show EC-dependent effects** when sensitive within-subjects designs with multiple input lists are used (1985), although the effects are small; and (3) a theoretical account (1988) of why the dissociation exists—the outshining hypothesis—explaining that recognition items are such powerful cues that environmental context is typically redundant and therefore shows little or no effect, whereas recall relies more heavily on contextual cues for retrieval. Related results (e.g., Smith et al., 1978) found significant context effects for recall but not recognition, and later meta-analytic work (Smith & Vela, 2001) confirmed that context effects are reliable overall (d = .28) but moderated by factors such as inter-item associative processing and test type, consistent with the outshining/cue-specificity framework.

## Summary: Fernandez & Glenberg (1985) — Failure of Environmental Context-Dependent Memory and Proposed Boundary Conditions

**The original study.** Fernandez and Glenberg (1985), "Changing environmental context does not reliably affect memory" (*Memory & Cognition*, 13, 333), reported **eight experiments that in aggregate challenged the reliability of the "same-context advantage"** (better memory when study and test environments match). Experiment 1 failed to obtain a same-context advantage; Experiments 2–7 manipulated various design features (e.g., identity of the experimenter at encoding/retrieval, learning task difficulty, serial position of stimuli) without producing a reliable effect; Experiment 8 repeated the methodology of a published report of a same-context advantage with more than double the number of subjects and still failed to replicate it. Across all experiments, no advantage of environmental reinstatement was found in over 300 subjects.

**Their proposed explanation — the "experimental context hypothesis."** Fernandez and Glenberg suggested that laboratory context manipulations are inherently ineffective because, from the subject's perspective, all environmental changes occur within the broader "experimental context." As they put it: "Laboratory tasks do not preserve the strong links between naturally occurring events and their environments that are presumed to underlie anecdotal reports of context effects," and "From the experimenter's point of view, changing the room produces a massive change in stimulation. The critical feature for the subject, however, may be that the events take place within the context of an experiment, and this feature does not change with a change of room." This overriding experimental context diminishes the salience of any environmental manipulation between study and test.

**Boundary conditions and explanations for their null results** (from later literature):

- **Associative processing at encoding (overshadowing).** A key proposed reason for Fernandez and Glenberg's failures is that participants were asked to **generate sentences incorporating target words**, which likely induced associative/inter-item processing during encoding. According to Smith and Vela's (2001) "overshadowing" principle, such non-environmental conceptual processing suppresses encoding of the environmental context, so reinstating the environment later has little effect.

- **Outshining at test.** The "outshining" hypothesis holds that when powerful non-environmental cues are available at retrieval (e.g., recognition test items or inter-item associations among list words), participants rely on those instead of environmental cues, reducing or eliminating context effects. Recognition tests are particularly prone to this; Fernandez and Glenberg tested both recall and recognition.

- **Stimulus familiarity.** A "familiarity hypothesis" (from face-recognition studies) argues that environmental context effects are robust for **novel stimuli** (e.g., novel faces) but disappear for **highly familiar stimuli** such as common words, which become "decontextualized" after repeated exposure in varied contexts. This could explain why Fernandez and Glenberg failed with word lists: words are familiar and thus less context-bound.

- **Mental reinstatement.** The "mental reinstatement" principle states that if participants mentally reinstate the encoding context at test, the physical context change matters little — a possibility in short-lag laboratory studies, and potentially influenced by demand characteristics if experimenters are not blind to condition.

- **Incidental vs. integral/influential contexts.** Bjork and Richardson-Klavehn (1988) suggested that only "integral" or "influential" environmental contexts (those tied to knowledge bases or needed to present stimuli) reliably affect memory; incidental contexts like room changes may not.

- **Realism.** The mood state-dependent memory meta-analysis noted that context effects depend on the realism of the experimental situation — subjects must perceive the context as causally belonging to the memory items — and argued that "the environment is in part what the subject makes it."

**Subsequent status.** Later work (e.g., Smith & Vela's 2001 meta-analysis) indicated that environmental reinstatement does aid both recall and recognition **when studies discourage inter-item associative processing**, effectively identifying the conditions under which Fernandez and Glenberg's null results occur. Their "experimental context hypothesis" has received some empirical support (e.g., Canas & Nelson, 1986, testing recognition over the telephone at home), though a similar paradigm (Wippich et al., 1985) also failed to produce effects, and the hypothesis cannot account for context effects found with novel faces within the experimental setting.

# State-Dependent Memory: Comparing Environmental, Mood, and Pharmacological Mechanisms (with Eich & Metcalfe's Contributions)

## Overview of the Three Domains

**Environmental context-dependent memory** refers to recall being better when the external setting at test matches the setting at encoding. The classic demonstration (Godden & Baddeley, 1975) involved divers studying material on land or underwater; participants recalled better when tested in the same environment where they studied.

**Pharmacological (drug) state-dependent memory** refers to recall depending on the match between internal physiological states at encoding and retrieval (e.g., studying while intoxicated and recalling better in the same drug state). Classic paradigms include Overton's (1964) T-maze study with pentobarbital in rats and human studies with marijuana and alcohol.

**Mood-dependent memory (MDM)** is analogous but with affective state: recall is improved when mood at encoding matches mood at retrieval. This must be distinguished from *mood-congruent memory*, which is the finding that stimuli are learned/remembered best when their emotional valence matches the current mood (e.g., depressed individuals better recalling negative words). Mood-dependence relates study and test moods to each other; mood congruence relates mood to stimulus valence.

## Eich and Metcalfe's Key Contributions

Eich (1980, 1989) and Eich & Metcalfe (1989, 1996) argued that state-dependent effects are reliable when two conditions are met:

1. **Cue-dependence**: State-dependent effects depend on the cues present at test. When memory tests provide good retrieval cues, effects are small or nonexistent. For example, marijuana-induced state dependence appeared in free recall but not category-cued recall (Eich et al., 1975; Eich, 1980). Similarly, cued recall and recognition tests were less likely than free recall to show state-dependent effects. Eich's (1980) "cue-dependent nature of state-dependent retrieval" holds that failures to demonstrate state dependence are restricted to situations where discretely identifiable retrieval cues are present.

2. **Reliable manipulation of internal states**: Effective drug doses are required—studies whose drug treatments had no measurable effects on acquisition or retention typically failed to show state dependence. For mood, Eich and Metcalfe (1989) developed a continuous music technique combining affectively valenced music with continuous self-report; participants studied/tested only after self-reports confirmed sufficient mood change.

**Eich & Metcalfe (1989)** tested whether internally generated events (reasoning, imagination, thought) are more colored by mood than externally sourced events. Using music-induced moods and generate/read procedures, they found that internal events are *less likely than external events* to be recalled after a mood shift—i.e., internally generated events show stronger mood dependence.

## Mechanistic Comparisons

**Cue-dependent retrieval**: In all three domains, internal states (drug, mood) or environmental contexts can serve as memory cues. When more effective external cues are available (e.g., category names), people do not use the less-effective internal cues. Eich (1989) hypothesized that the mechanisms responsible for internal state-dependent memory are the same as those for external context-dependent memory.

**State-modulation hypothesis**: External context may affect memory by inducing consistent internal states. Since all configurations of external stimuli occur in internal states, reinstating an external context may reinstate the internal state present at encoding—thus environmental context effects could be mediated by internal states. Conversely, Eich (1995) argued that "place-dependent" effects may be mediated by mood alterations.

**Search set activation**: Environmental context may help retrieval by including contextual associations in the memory search set (following Shiffrin's 1970 model). This mechanism matters in free recall but is less important in recognition, where targets are supplied externally.

**Direct context-to-item associations**: Models like SAM propose direct associations between contextual representations and target information, predicting familiarity-based effects when input and test contexts match.

**Contextual fluctuation and drift**: Bower's contextual drift hypothesis holds that the active set of encoding operators fluctuates over time, so matching cognitive operations are less likely to be active with greater delays. Menne and Raaijmakers incorporated stochastic contextual fluctuation into SAM. Glenberg's component-levels theory distinguishes descriptive (item-specific), structural (associative), and contextual (general) components, with contextual cues being the most overloaded and weakest.

**Cue overload**: The more targets associated with a cue, the weaker the cue. Context cues are associated with all targets and are therefore the weakest—consistent with findings that single-context learning produces poorer recall than varied-context learning (Smith, 1982, 1994).

**Outshining**: Context effects may be hidden when other, more salient cues are available at test—a psychophysical metaphor (a dim star is invisible with background light but visible in darkness). This explains why good cues at test diminish state/context dependence.

## Task Sensitivity as a Unifying Comparison

Across all three domains, the same pattern emerges: **free recall is sensitive to state/context match, while cued recall and recognition are not**. The marijuana study (Eich, 1980) showed impairment from state change in free recall but not category-cued recall. Eich & Birnbaum (1982) showed that repetition and category-name cuing enhance accessibility of higher-order units and diminish the extent to which access to these units is state dependent. The Quizlet summary of Bower, Eich, and Metcalfe's mood study likewise found free recall improved when mood states matched, regardless of the emotional valence of recalled events.

## Additional Pharmacological Considerations

- **Asymmetric effects**: A drug that normally impairs memory (e.g., alcohol) can enhance memory if the material was learned in that drug state.
- **Effective dose requirement**: State dependence requires drug treatments that actually affect acquisition or retention.
- **Time course**: State-dependency effects (including drug-induced) are strongest shortly after learning and weaken with longer retention intervals.
- **Reconsolidation**: State-dependency can be integrated into memories during reactivation; supposedly amnestic agents given at reactivation may actually induce state-dependence, such that memory appears only when tested in the same drug state (relevant to Eich's framework of state-specific memory).

## Summary

The core comparison is that environmental context, mood, and pharmacological states all operate through the same fundamental mechanism—**the match between internal and/or external states at encoding and retrieval serves as a retrieval cue**—but their effects are conditional on (a) the reliability/strength of the state manipulation and (b) the availability of alternative, stronger cues at test. Eich and Metcalfe's work is central to this framework, establishing that internal events are more mood-dependent than external events, that reliable mood induction (music + self-report) is essential, and that state-dependent effects are cue-dependent rather than automatic.

# Smith (1979) Mental Reinstatement Study: Imagining the Room and Free Recall

## Overview

Steven M. Smith's 1979 study, *"Remembering In and Out of Context"* (published in the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory*, Vol. 5, pp. 460–471), examined how environmental context affects memory. Across three experiments with 120 college students, Smith demonstrated the **environmental reinstatement effect**: participants recall more when tested in their original learning environment than when tested in a new one. Crucially, the study showed that **mentally reinstating the learning context (imagining the room) can be as effective as physically being in that room** for free recall.

## Key Experiments and Findings

**Experiment 1** ruled out the alternative explanation that the context effect was merely a performance decrement caused by the unfamiliarity of a new test room. Participants learned words in Room A, were familiarized with another room (or not), and were tested in the same room, a familiar-but-different room, or an unfamiliar room. The same-context group (ABA) recalled significantly more words (mean 24.0) than the mismatched groups (ABB: 18.5; ACB: 17.7), with no effect of room familiarity — supporting the memory-based (contextual association) explanation over the performance hypothesis.

**Experiment 2** tested whether participants could overcome context dependence through **mental reinstatement**. Participants tested in a new room were instructed to recall/think about the original learning environment just prior to free recall of list words. The results showed that this **mental reinstatement completely eliminated the context effect**: different-context participants who were told to remember the study room (with or without a picture as an aid) recalled as many words as the same-context group. In other words, **imagining the original room was as effective as actually being in it**.

**Experiment 3** showed that this "release from contextual dependence" was diminished when the original learning room was made more difficult to remember. Participants who encountered many competing contexts (five rooms) showed a clear same-context advantage, whereas those who encountered only two contexts could easily internally reinstate the encoding room and compensate for the lack of external cues.

## Conclusions

Smith concluded that **context effects can be brought under cognitive control**: participants can supply their own contextual retrieval cues when the original context can be easily recalled. This mental reinstatement effect — essentially "closing your eyes and imagining being back in the original study room" — was as effective for free recall as physical context reinstatement. This finding is widely cited as the basis for the mental reinstatement of context component used in the cognitive interview technique for eyewitness memory.

# Varied Practice vs. Consistent Context Study: The Encoding Specificity–Desirable Difficulties Trade-off

The research on this question reveals a genuine tension between two well-established principles of memory, with the key insight being that the trade-off depends on *what kind of learning* you want (durable and transferable vs. context-bound and fragile) and *what learning activity* you're doing (restudying vs. retrieval practice).

## The Two Principles in Tension

**Encoding specificity** (Tulving & Thompson, 1973) holds that memory is stored as a web of contextual associations—retrieval is best when the retrieval context matches the encoding context (podcast episode on "The Encoding Retrieval Gap"). This predicts that studying in the exam room (or in the same context as the test) should boost performance, because environmental cues present during study are re-presented at test. Godden & Baddeley's (1975) classic scuba diver study showed cross-context recall dropped by ~40%.

**Desirable difficulties** (Bjork, 1994) predict the opposite: *varying* the conditions of practice, rather than keeping them constant and predictable, produces more durable and flexible learning, even though it makes immediate performance worse (Bjork & Bjork essay; Knowledge Hub). Robert and Elizabeth Bjork explicitly note that studying the same material in **two different rooms rather than twice in the same room** leads to increased recall (Smith, Glenberg & Bjork, 1978)—"an empirical result that flies in the face of the common how-to-study suggestion to find a quiet, convenient place and do all your studying there."

## The Core Trade-off

- **Consistent context study** (e.g., always studying in the exam room): When instruction occurs under constrained, predictable conditions, learning becomes *contextualized*. Material is easily retrieved in that context, but the learning "does not support later performance if tested at a delay, in a different context, or both" (Bjork & Bjork). The stable context acts as an additional retrieval cue, making recall easier but "more superficial"—the knowledge is never disentangled from the context in which it was practiced (Kirschner-ED, contextual interference article).

- **Varied practice**: Deliberately learning/practicing in multiple contexts forces learners to rely less on environmental cues and more on memory itself, producing retrieval that is "less fluent, and more effortful, but also more productive" (Kirschner-ED). This is why varied practice is classified as a *desirable* difficulty—it sacrifices short-term performance for long-term retention and transfer.

The Kerr & Booth (1978) beanbag study is the canonical demonstration: children who practiced throwing to *varied* distances outperformed children who practiced at the exact tested distance, even when tested at that distance—the benefits of variation outweighed the benefit of practice-test matching.

## The Critical Nuance: It Depends on the Learning Activity

The most relevant recent evidence—Imundo, Pan, Bjork & Bjork (2020), *"Where and How to Learn"*—reveals an important interaction between context variation and retrieval practice:

- **Restudying in a new context** did *not* impair recall and in one experiment *significantly enhanced* it—consistent with the varied-practice benefit.
- **Testing/retrieval practice in a new context** significantly *reduced* recall (participants in the same-context test condition recalled more than twice as much during Session 2; final test performance was .37 vs. .18 for varied-context testers), and this impairment carried over to the final test.

The researchers interpret this as consistent with a "distribution-of-memory-strengths" framework: when you test yourself in a new context, the retrieval attempt is more likely to fail, and **failed retrieval without feedback** can be harmful. Their practical recommendations: study in more than one environmental setting; but when engaging in retrieval practice, either ensure a high level of successful retrieval or make feedback available for errors (TeacherToolkit summary).

## Why This Matters for Exam Performance

The tension is partly an illusion created by short-term measures. Kirschner-ED's contextual interference piece explains that many "assessment failures aren't learning failures but transfer failures": when a test strips away the contextual supports that made performance possible during learning, what remains is the knowledge itself—and too often that knowledge was never required to stand on its own. "Teaching to the test" (matching study and exam contexts) can appear effective in the short term but fails on cumulative exams, later courses, or real-world application; "this isn't transfer; it's alignment."

The Bjork framework (storage strength vs. retrieval strength) explains why: consistent-context study inflates *retrieval strength* (easy access right now, in that context) without building robust *storage strength* (durable encoding). Retrieval strength "is usually higher in familiar environments, with familiar cues"—which is exactly why studying in the exam room *feels* effective. But high retrieval strength is a poor signal of durable learning, and learners systematically misread it (Structural Learning article; Simon & Bjork, 2001).

## Caveats and Boundary Conditions

1. **Desirable difficulties are only *desirable* when the learner can respond to them successfully** (Bjork & Bjork). For true novices with insufficient background knowledge, too much contextual variation becomes overwhelming and "destructive rather than productive"—contextual stability may be necessary early on, but "should never be the end point" (Kirschner-ED).
2. **High-element-interactivity materials** (complex, interrelated content) may convert desirable difficulties into *undesirable* ones, because the added difficulty strains already-stressed working memory (PMC/Frontiers in Psychology article).
3. **Varied practice can hurt on recognition tests**—Smith et al. (1978) found the varied-context advantage on free recall but a reversed effect on recognition, so the benefit is not universal (PMC article).

## Bottom Line

The research suggests the trade-off should be resolved in favor of **varied practice as the default strategy**, because it produces the durable, transferable learning that exams (ideally) measure—while recognizing that consistent-context study is a short-term crutch. If you know the exam context, matching it can temporarily boost retrieval, but that boost is fragile and context-dependent. The most defensible approach per the evidence: **vary your study contexts** (even simple room changes help), and if you engage in retrieval practice, be aware that testing in a novel context reduces performance—so ensure feedback or a high initial success rate to avoid cementing failures. The exam room itself should not be the only or primary study context, because knowledge that survives context change is the knowledge that was truly learned.

## Godden & Baddeley (1980): Recognition Failure of Environmental Context Effects

**The study:** In their paper *"When does context influence recognition memory?"* (British Journal of Psychology, 71(1), 99–104, 1980), Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley followed up on their classic 1975 finding that environmental context strongly influences **free recall** (divers recalled words better when tested in the same environment — land or underwater — where they had learned them). The 1980 study asked whether the same context-dependency would appear with a **recognition** test.

**Method:** Drawing on Hewitt's (1977) distinction between *intrinsic context* (directly involved in encoding the material) and *extrinsic context* (arbitrary environmental features such as the learning surroundings), the researchers used the highly contrasting land versus underwater environments. Divers learned lists of 36 words either on land or underwater, then tried to recognize them from a list of 72 words presented in either the same or the alternative environment.

**Key finding — a dissociation:** In contrast to the earlier recall study, **no trace of context dependency was observed for recognition**. Participants recognized words equally well regardless of whether testing occurred in the same or a different environment from learning. In other words, environmental context had a strong effect on free recall but no effect on recognition — a classic dissociation demonstrating that the presence or absence of contextual cues only affects memory when it is tested via recall rather than recognition.

**Implications:**
- The results support the intrinsic/extrinsic context distinction: recognition effects are observed with intrinsic context but not with extrinsic/environmental context.
- In the memory literature (e.g., Baddeley's own textbook, and subsequent evaluation of retrieval-failure theory), this is cited as a limitation of context-dependent forgetting — context effects depend substantially on the type of memory being tested, so retrieval failure due to absent environmental cues does not fully explain forgetting.
- Practically, the finding mattered for divers' training and debriefing: while free recall underwater was poor, recognition was unimpaired (and cued recall was less disrupted than free recall), which is why underwater tape-recorded commentaries were recommended.

# Summary: Smith (2013) "Effects of Environmental Context on Human Memory" in *The SAGE Handbook of Applied Memory*

Steven M. Smith's chapter, **"Effects of Environmental Context on Human Memory"** (2013), appears in *The SAGE Handbook of Applied Memory*, edited by Timothy J. Perfect and D. Stephen Lindsay (SAGE, 2013, ISBN 9781446208427, 752 pages). The chapter is located in **Part One: Everyday Memory** and begins on page 162.

## Chapter Content

**Introduction and Core Questions.** The chapter opens with the observation that returning to a place after many years can revive seemingly lost memories, and that remembering experiences often begins with recalling *where* we were. The chapter addresses two central questions: How do the environmental contexts of experiences affect what we learn and remember, and how can understanding of environmental context-dependent memory be used to benefit people?

**Defining Environmental Context.** Smith defines an *environment* as one's physical surroundings—the immediately perceptible and navigable space in which one is immersed. While no single object or stimulus constitutes an environment, collections of objects and stimuli can form important environmental elements. The *environmental context* is specifically a mental representation of a place, which can be instantiated by a physically present environment, a remembered one, one cued by stimuli (e.g., photos, video, virtual reality), or an imagined one. Smith notes that although stimuli like color, font, mood state, and associated words can be elements of episodic contexts, they are not places where experiences occur, nor do they reliably trigger place representations as pictures or movies do. The chapter focuses on places associated with events and their effects on learning and memory.

**Historical Overview.** The chapter reviews a century of experimental psychology research on environmental context effects, noting a "steady trickle" of studies, sometimes conducted in colorful and imaginative ways. Smith observes that there has never been consensus on the operational definition of environmental context; historically, definitions have tended to center on *global types of context*—contexts common to entire episodes—though notable exceptions exist (citing Dulsky, 1935, and Pan, 1926). The earliest context-dependent memory studies began with non-human animals (a research area that continues to burgeon), with interest quickly turning to humans. The chapter then provides a historical review of twentieth-century research on environmental context effects on human memory.

**Scope of Coverage.** The chapter reviews the long history of investigations across varied operational definitions, discusses theoretical treatments of contextual influences on memory, and describes applied uses of context cues—primarily in **education, aging, clinical applications, and eyewitness memory**. It concludes with discussion of as-yet-unanswered questions about environmental context and memory.

## Handbook Context

The *SAGE Handbook of Applied Memory* is described as the first of its kind to focus specifically on applied memory research. It is organized into four sections: Everyday Memory; Social and Individual Differences in Memory; Subjective Experience of Memory; and Eyewitness Memory. The handbook is praised by Elizabeth F. Loftus as "a fabulous collection of essays on memory in the real world" and by Graham Davies (Editor, *Applied Cognitive Psychology*) as "an invaluable resource for anyone wishing to access the current state of knowledge of, or contemplating research into, the growing area of applied memory research." Other chapters in the Everyday Memory section include the Testing Effect (McDermott, Arnold, & Nelson), Forgetting (Kelley), Memory and Emotion (Fiedler & Hutter), and False Memory (Newman & Garry), among others.

## Summary: Murre (2021) Replication of the Godden & Baddeley (1975) Diving Study

**Citation:** Murre, J. M. J. (2021). "The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication." *Royal Society Open Science*, 8(11), 200724. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.200724 (Published online 3 November 2021; PMID: 34760281)

### Study Design
Jaap Murre (University of Amsterdam) attempted a direct replication of the classic Godden & Baddeley (1975) experiment on environmental context-dependent memory. Sixteen experienced divers (average age 29.5; 10 men, 6 women) studied auditorily presented Dutch word lists either on land (Dry) or underwater (Wet) and recalled them 4 minutes later in either environment, with each diver completing all four combinations (Dry–Dry, Dry–Wet, Wet–Dry, Wet–Wet). The experiment took place in a single day in a heated indoor swimming pool (~180 cm deep) in Amsterdam, rather than the open water used in the original study.

### Key Results
- **Failure to replicate:** Contrary to the original study, Murre did **not** find that recall was better in the same context where words were learned. The crucial interaction between learning and recall environment was not statistically significant (F = 1.999, df1 = 1, df2 = 60, p = 0.163).
- There was a main effect of learning environment (F = 16.2, p < 0.001)—words learned on land were recalled better overall—but no main effect of recall environment.
- Detailed comparisons showed no difference between same- versus different-context recall overall (p = 0.215). Notably, when words were learned underwater, recall on land was actually *better* than recall underwater (p < 0.01)—a trend opposite to the original finding.

### Differences from the Original Study Discussed by the Author
Murre noted several procedural and environmental differences that may explain the null result:
- The original divers completed the four conditions over 4 days, whereas Murre's participants did all four in about 1.5 hours, potentially causing proactive interference.
- The replication used a shallow, heated indoor pool rather than cold open water at ~7 m depth, so the contextual contrast was much smaller.
- The experiment was filmed for a Dutch TV programme (with celebrity Katja Schuurman participating, though her data were excluded), which may have been distracting.
- Overall recall scores were lower, possibly due to more difficult words or an older, less homogeneous sample.

### Reviewer Critiques (from the review history)
One reviewer argued the replication was not a close, robust, or valid replication, citing the much smaller difference between environments (pool edge vs. 6-foot depth versus 20 feet of water on a busy beach), same-day testing of all conditions, group testing (groups of four vs. pairs), the TV filming, and differences in participant populations. The reviewer suggested the original effect may reflect not simply being underwater but the dramatic difference between environments.

### 2022 Addendum (Correction/Reanalysis)
A subsequent addendum (Murre, 2022, *R. Soc. Open Sci.* 9(1), 211924, https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.211924) acknowledged that the original analysis should have used a repeated measures ANOVA with order as a between-subjects covariate, as identified by Sean Mackinnon. A minor data-entry error (a value of 14 that should have been 13) was also corrected. Under this reanalysis, the Learn × Recall interaction became statistically significant (p = 0.017), and the three-way Learn × Recall × Order interaction just reached significance (p = 0.045). However, the addendum concludes that this **reinforces** the conclusion that the study was **not a successful replication** of Godden & Baddeley (1975), because the pattern of results (e.g., Dry–Dry and Wet–Wet conditions not being highest) differed from what a successful replication would show.

### Broader Significance
The paper received results-blind in-principle acceptance at *Royal Society Open Science* and was preregistered on the OSF. Murre emphasized the importance of attempting replications of classic, widely cited studies, noting this was the first published replication attempt of the Godden & Baddeley diving experiment (per Alan Baddeley, personal communication in 2014, no prior replications were known). The data are publicly available at https://osf.io/q2vjk/.

## Smith, Glenberg, & Bjork (1978): "Environmental Context and Human Memory"

**Citation:** Smith, S.M., Glenberg, A.M., & Bjork, R.A. (1978). Environmental context and human memory. *Memory & Cognition*, 6(4), 342–353. DOI: 10.3758/bf03197465

### Overview
This landmark paper reported **five experiments** examining how environmental context affects recall and recognition. It is frequently cited as an illustration of the **encoding specificity principle** (Tulving & Thomson, 1973): memory is improved when information available at encoding is also available at retrieval—for example, when people are tested in the same room where they studied versus a different room.

### Key Findings from the Experiments
- **Experiment 1 (the classic "varied rooms" effect):** Participants studied a word list twice, either in the same room both times or in two different rooms (one a cluttered basement, the other a windowed office). Three hours later, they were tested in a third "neutral" room. Those who studied in the same room recalled an average of **16 out of 40 words**, whereas those who studied in two different rooms recalled **24 words**—demonstrating that **variability of input environments produced higher free recall** than unchanged environments. This became known as the **"variation effect"** (or environmental enrichment effect).
- **Experiment 2:** Showed improvements in cued recall when storage and test contexts matched, using a paradigm that unconfounded the variables of context mismatching and context change.
- **Experiment 3:** Recall of categories and of words within a category was better in same-context than different-context recall.
- **Recognition experiments:** Subjects given identical input conditions showed strong environmental context effects on free recall but **no main effects of context on recognition tests**; this null recognition effect was replicated using a cued recognition task to control semantic encodings. The authors interpreted this as indicating that environmental context influences memory processes tied to retrieval, not recognition-based familiarity.

### Significance and Influence
- The study is foundational for research on **context-dependent memory** and is often cited in educational contexts to support the recommendation that students study in varied locations rather than one fixed spot.
- **Caveats from later research:** Lefebvre, Lefebvre, & Standing (2011) noted that the 1978 Experiment 1 **confounded room change with modality change** (visual presentation in the first room, auditory in the second) and used only 16 subjects. Their replication, using short retention intervals (~17 min) and separating room and modality factors, failed to find the enrichment effect, suggesting the benefit may depend on longer consolidation intervals.
- **Modern replication:** Imundo et al. (2020, Bjork lab) partially replicated the finding across multi-day intervals, concluding that restudying in varied contexts produced better final recall than restudying in the same context—supporting the contextual variation benefit, while also finding complex interactions with retrieval practice.

# Tulving's Encoding Specificity Principle: Retrieval Cue Mechanisms, Memory Traces, and Theoretical Debates

## The Principle and Its Core Claims

Endel Tulving's **encoding specificity principle (ESP)**, formalized with Donald Thomson in the landmark 1973 paper *"Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory"*, holds that "specific encoding operations performed on what is perceived determine what is stored, and what is stored determines what retrieval cues are effective in providing access to what is stored" (Tulving & Thomson, 1973, p. 359). A more precise later formulation (Tulving, 1979) states that "the probability of successful retrieval of the target item is a monotonically increasing function of informational overlap between the information present at retrieval and the information stored in memory." The principle was developed to explain the effect of extralist cuing and, especially, the puzzling phenomenon of **recognition failure of recallable words**—cases where subjects consistently failed to recognize many words they could nonetheless recall. ESP accounts for this by arguing that the memory trace of an event, and hence the properties of an effective retrieval cue, are determined by the specific encoding operations performed on the input.

## Retrieval Cue Mechanism and the Engram

ESP radically reframed the retrieval cue mechanism. Rather than a cue acting as a pointer that locates a stored trace (as in generation-recognition and library-like theories), Tulving proposed that **retrieval is a constructive interaction between the cue and the engram**. This process was termed **eephory** (or *synergistic eephory*), a term Tulving adopted from the German psychologist Richard Semon, who also coined the term *engram* for the memory trace as a biological entity. Eephory "combines information from the engram and from the retrieval environment, and converts it into eephoric information" that underlies recollective experience. In Tulving's account, the engram is not a copy of experience waiting to be found; rather, "engrams are dispositions, potentialities, processes held in abeyance" that can only be made manifest in interaction with a relevant cue. Flexser and Tulving (1978) specified that both engrams and retrieval cues consist of bundles of features, with informational overlap determined by the number of matching features.

The classic experimental demonstration was Thomson and Tulving (1970): to-be-remembered words studied with weakly associated cues (e.g., "Train–BLACK") were recalled best when those same weak cues were provided at test; recall dropped when strong normative associates (e.g., "White–BLACK") were substituted, even though strong cues generally facilitate retrieval. The effectiveness of a retrieval cue thus "varies directly with the extent it matches the format of the to-be-remembered information stored in memory." Tulving's approach also introduced the influential **availability versus accessibility** distinction (from Tulving & Pearlstone, 1966): memory failure often reflects a retrieval/accessibility problem, not a loss of stored information—as in cue-dependent forgetting, where the trace remains intact but cannot be evoked by an insufficient cue. Tulving speculated that cue-dependent forgetting may be "the general rule" of forgetting.

## Theoretical Debate and Criticisms

The results supporting ESP were "fiercely disputed" when first published (later, colleagues claimed they were "obvious and trite"). Key debates identified in the sources include:

1. **Circularity/untestability**: Solso's famous critique—"If a cue was effective in memory retrieval, then one could infer it was encoded; if a cue was not effective, then it was not encoded. The logic of this theorization is 'heads I win, tails you lose'"—remains the standard objection. Because Tulving allows that cues may be encoded implicitly without experimenter manipulation, the principle is difficult to falsify. Tulving defended it by analogy to untestable principles like Darwinian natural selection.

2. **The "if and only if" clause**: ESP's strict claim that cues facilitate recall *if and only if* their information was stored with the target was challenged by demonstrations that extralist cues (not present at encoding but strongly pre-experimentally associated with targets) can be effective (e.g., Anderson & Pichert, 1978; Kochevar & Fox, 1980). Postman (1975) found constraints on the principle's generality, concluding that high-association cues are still more effective in some conditions, suggesting a compromise with generation-recognition theory.

3. **Failure to specify cue effectiveness**: Critics (e.g., Kim, 1986) argued that ESP defines the effectiveness of *eephoric information*, not of the retrieval cue itself, and does not specify what determines the amount or kind of compatibility, since Tulving admitted "no one yet knows the nature" of the eephory interaction.

4. **De-emphasis of retrieval strategies**: Eysenck noted that Tulving treats retrieval cues as entering eephory "directly without any intervening process," neglecting the variety of retrieval strategies (inference, generation of candidates) that cues can instigate; an indirect route of recall may explain why strong recall cues were effective even after weak-cue encoding.

5. **Episodic-semantic distinction**: ESP is closely tied to Tulving's episodic/semantic memory distinction, itself heavily debated (e.g., by Anderson & Ross, Baddeley, McKoon & Ratcliff, Roediger). Critics argued the distinction is neither necessary for ESP nor for explaining retrieval phenomena.

6. **Theoretical elaborations**: Tulving's later General Abstract Processing System (GAPS) and Synergistic Eephory Model added processes of *conversion* (turning eephoric information/recollective experience into overt behavior) and retrieval mode, positing different conversion thresholds for recall versus recognition. Critics found the addition of conversion inadequately motivated and noted inconsistencies in Tulving's "semi-constructive" view—e.g., assuming the trace is not changed during retrieval, which contradicts his own claims about recoding.

## Retrieval-Only Emphasis and Modern Neurobiological Evidence

A striking theme across the sources is that ESP made **retrieval the central, defining process of memory**. As Craik notes, retrieval was largely ignored before the 1960s; Tulving's work—starting with free-recall experiments—forced consideration of retrieval mechanisms. Roediger's remark captures the position: "Encoding and storage are necessary but certainly not sufficient conditions for remembering: retrieval processes are critical to convert these latent traces to conscious mental experience of the past." Moscovitch similarly argued that "memory does not exist until it is revealed in behavior or thought." Tulving's view entails that attempts by neurophysiologists to "find the engram" are doomed, since what could be found is only "a changed tendency in some neural network to yield a specific experience when combined with the appropriate cue."

Modern neuroscience has nonetheless pursued the engram, with results that both support and refine ESP. Frankland, Josselyn, and Köhler (2019) review how optogenetic tagging in rodents has made eephory experimentally tractable: silencing engram ensembles prevents retrieval despite natural cues; direct photostimulation of engrams induces memory expression without natural cues; and "silent engrams" (available but inaccessible by natural means) can be recovered by artificial reactivation—providing a biological analogue of Tulving's availability/accessibility distinction. Jung et al. (2023) directly tested the "engram encoding specificity hypothesis" in mice, finding that retrieval conditions closely matching training conditions produce maximal engram reactivation and recall, providing "a biological basis for the encoding specificity hypothesis" and confirming that "memory recall involves an interaction between stored information (engram) and information available at retrieval (the memory retrieval cue)."

## Summary

In short, Tulving's encoding specificity principle holds that retrieval cues are effective only to the extent that they match the specific way information was encoded into the memory trace (engram); retrieval is an interactive, constructive process (synergistic eephory) rather than mere trace location, and memory failure is often a problem of accessibility (cue insufficiency) rather than availability (storage loss). The principle sparked enduring theoretical debates—over circularity, the strict "if and only if" claim, the specification of cue effectiveness, and the episodic-semantic distinction—while also establishing retrieval as the pivotal process in memory research, a position now receiving convergent support from engram-level neuroscience.

# Environmental Context-Dependent Memory: Effect Sizes, Recall–Recognition Dissociation, and the Outshining Hypothesis

## The Meta-Analysis and Effect Sizes

The foundational work here is **Smith and Vela's (2001) meta-analysis**, "Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis" (*Psychonomic Bulletin & Review*). They reviewed nearly a century of research on incidental environmental context-dependent memory, calculating **93 effect sizes from 75 experiments reported in 41 published articles (1935–1997)**. The average weighted effect size was **d = .28 — a modest but reliable effect** of environmental context on memory. Moderators mattered: studies with **longer retention intervals produced significantly larger effect sizes** than shorter intervals, and studies encouraging **non-associative processing at study averaged d = .33**, whereas those encouraging **associative encoding averaged only d = .13** (a significantly smaller effect).

## The Recall–Recognition Dissociation

A classic puzzle in the literature was that early experiments found **robust environmental context effects for recall but not for recognition** (e.g., Godden & Baddeley, 1980; Smith, Glenberg, & Bjork, 1978). The Sage Handbook chapter explicitly notes that Smith et al. (1978) found a significant context effect for recall but not recognition, as did Godden and Baddeley (1980). This apparent dissociation is central to the theoretical debate.

However, the Smith and Vela (2001) meta-analysis **did not support a simple recall–recognition split**: significant positive context effects were found for **both recall and recognition**, indicating that "finding incidental environmental context-dependent memory effects depends on principles that were less obvious than the type of memory test used." Relatedly, a Quizlet summary of the paper states that "there was not a significant effect of the type of memory test (i.e., free recall, cued recall, or recognition)" in the meta-analysis. The recognition effects in the meta-analysis were partly driven by **unfamiliar or meaningless materials** (e.g., unfamiliar faces, nonwords), which produced large context-dependent recognition effects, and by problematic studies; for meaningful words, recognition effects were equivocal. Follow-up work (Isarida et al., 2012) showed context-dependent recognition of meaningful words emerges with **short study time (1.5 s/item)** but disappears with **long study time (4.0 s/item)**, whereas nonwords show context effects even at long study times.

## The Outshining Hypothesis (Theoretical Explanation)

The **outshining hypothesis** (Smith, 1988, 1994) is the primary theoretical explanation for the recall–recognition dissociation. It holds that:

- **Environmental cues are encoded by default**, but at test, if **non-contextual cues are available and used**, they can "outshine" (overwhelm) the relatively weak ambient environmental cues, diminishing or eliminating context effects.
- **Recognition tests provide more non-contextual cues than recall tests**: the test item itself, plus reinstated inter-item associations and subjective organizations from study, serve as powerful retrieval cues. Thus, the outshining hypothesis predicts **less incidental context dependence for cued recall than free recall, and even less for recognition**.
- The account combines **encoding specificity** (Tulving & Thomson, 1973) with the outshining principle: item cue strength increases with **material meaningfulness and study time**, so item cues are more likely to outshine context cues as these increase. This explains why context-dependent recognition disappears with meaningful words at long study times but appears with nonwords or brief study times.

In the Smith and Vela meta-analysis, the outshining hypothesis was **supported** in that "the use of non-contextual cues during learning (overshadowing) and at test (outshining), as well as mental reinstatement of appropriate context cues at test, all reduce the effect of environmental manipulations." However, the specific prediction that test type (recall vs. recognition) would modulate effects was **not confirmed** in the meta-analysis.

## Related Theoretical Mechanisms

The full theoretical framework (Smith & Vela, 2001) rests on Glenberg's (1997) contention that **introspective thought requires cognitive resources normally used to represent the immediate environment** — so conceptual processing suppresses the environment. Four hypotheses were tested:

1. **Reinstatement**: environmental context effects are reliable overall (supported).
2. **Outshining**: non-contextual cues at test suppress use of ambient context (supported, though test-type moderation was not significant).
3. **Overshadowing**: suppression of the environment during learning prevents encoding/storage of contextual information (partially supported — associative processing at input diminished context dependence, but time-in-context did not predict effect magnitude, contrary to prediction).
4. **Mental reinstatement**: subjects mentally reinstating learning contexts at test reduces ambient context effects (clearly supported — reinstatement instructions improved memory, and first-order reinstatement paradigms yielded less context dependence than second-order paradigms).

## Alternative/Complementary Explanations

- **ICE theory** (Murnane, Phelps, & Malmberg, 1999): explains context-dependent recognition via global activation of item (I), context (C), and ensemble (E) information; context-dependent discrimination emerges only when item and context are integrated into an "ensemble." However, the Isarida review argues place-, background-music-, and background-color-dependent recognition are better explained by the **encoding specificity principle plus an auxiliary principle** — the **outshining principle** (for place and music) or the **cue-overload principle** (for background color).
- **Cue overload** (Watkins & Watkins, 1975): context effects disappear when too many items are associated with a single context cue (e.g., one background color for all items), because the cue is overloaded.
- **Dual-process recognition** research shows *remember* responses (recollection) reveal context-dependent recognition discrimination while *know* responses (familiarity) do not, though this has been questioned.

## Conclusion

In sum, the meta-analytic evidence shows environmental context has a **modest but reliable effect on memory (d ≈ .28)**, with effects present in both recall and recognition under the right conditions. The classic **recall–recognition dissociation** (robust context effects in recall, absent in recognition) is best explained by the **outshining hypothesis**: recognition tests supply strong item-based, non-contextual cues that outshine the weaker environmental context cues, unless materials are unfamiliar/meaningless or study time is brief. Overshadowing at encoding and mental reinstatement are complementary mechanisms that also reduce environmental context dependence, consistent with the view that context effects occur unless the immediate environment is suppressed.

## CONTRADICTIONS

**Contradiction 1: Effect size of contextual reinstatement — gigantic vs modest.**
Godden & Baddeley (1975) implies a Cohen's d of ~2.71 — an enormous effect. The Smith & Vela (2001) meta-analysis finds an average d = 0.28 — small-to-modest. Murre (2021) fails to replicate entirely. Resolution: the Godden & Baddeley effect was amplified by an extreme environmental contrast (cold open sea at depth vs sunny beach) that is unlike typical lab room changes. The meta-analytic average better represents the true effect under typical conditions. The original effect — even if real at that magnitude — is not the typical case.

**Contradiction 2: Does varied context help or hurt?**
Smith, Glenberg & Bjork (1978) found that studying in two different rooms improved recall (24/40 vs 16/40). The encoding specificity principle predicts that matching study-test context should help. Resolution: the two principles operate on different aspects of memory. Varied encoding builds richer, less context-bound representations (a storage-strength benefit). Matched retrieval context provides additional cues (a retrieval-strength boost). The varied-context benefit is for long-term retention and transfer; the matched-context benefit is for immediate, context-bound performance. Imundo et al. (2020) add the crucial insight that retrieval practice in a changed context is harmful (failed retrievals get consolidated), while restudying in a changed context is beneficial.

**Contradiction 3: Recall–recognition dissociation — is it real?**
Godden & Baddeley (1980) and Smith et al. (1978) found clear recall-only effects. Fernandez & Glenberg (1985) found nothing at all. The Smith & Vela (2001) meta-analysis reports significant positive effects for both recall and recognition, contradicting the simple dissociation. Resolution: recognition effects do occur, but only under specific conditions — unfamiliar/meaningless materials, short study times (1.5s/item, not 4.0s/item; Isarida et al. 2012), or when inter-item associative processing is discouraged. The dissociation is quantitative (recognition effects are much smaller and harder to detect) rather than qualitative, and is explained by the outshining hypothesis.

**Contradiction 4: Fernandez & Glenberg (1985) null results vs positive meta-analytic effect.**
Eight experiments, N>300, no context effect found. But the meta-analysis finds d=0.28 reliably across 75 experiments. Resolution: Fernandez & Glenberg used sentence-generation encoding tasks that induced inter-item associative processing, which the meta-analysis identifies as a key suppressor of context effects (d=0.13 vs d=0.33 for non-associative encoding). Their null results may be a procedural artifact rather than evidence against the phenomenon.

---

## OPEN GAPS

1. **Ecological validity of lab contexts.** The "experimental context hypothesis" (Fernandez & Glenberg 1985) — that subjects perceive all lab rooms as the same experimental context — remains untested in a systematic way. Do context effects emerge only when environments are perceived as semantically distinct (not just perceptually different)? Virtual reality could be used to parametrically vary environmental distinctiveness.

2. **The interaction between context variation and retrieval practice.** Imundo et al. (2020) found that varied-context restudying is beneficial but varied-context retrieval practice is harmful. This interaction needs replication and mechanistic explanation. If confirmed, it has major pedagogical implications: students should vary study locations for reading/review but NOT for self-testing — unless feedback is always provided.

3. **The role of internal state in mediating environmental context effects.** Does environmental context change work because external cues change, or because the external change triggers a change in internal state (mood, arousal, physiological state)? Smith (2013) raises this but it remains unresolved. A study independently manipulating environment and internal state would be needed.

4. **Neurobiological mechanism of environmental context reinstatement.** While engram-level studies (Jung et al. 2023) have shown encoding specificity at the neuronal ensemble level in mice, no human neuroimaging study has directly tested whether physically returning to a room reactivates hippocampal place-context representations that were active during encoding.

5. **Individual differences.** Are some people more context-dependent than others? Field dependence (Witkin) was tested inconclusively by Smith (1985). Working memory capacity, age, and expertise might moderate context dependence. Older adults may be more context-dependent (Smith & Vela 2001 meta-analysis mentions age as a potential moderator but data were sparse).

6. **Duration of the context reinstatement effect.** Most studies use retention intervals of minutes to hours. Does the effect survive days, weeks, or years? Smith & Vela (2001) found that longer delays produced larger effects — puzzling and counterintuitive. This needs systematic investigation.

7. **Mental reinstatement boundary conditions.** Smith (1979) showed mental reinstatement fails when the encoding context is difficult to remember (many competing contexts). What other factors determine mental reinstatement success? The cognitive interview literature provides practical guidance but the underlying mechanisms are poorly specified.

8. **The Godden & Baddeley (1975) replication crisis.** Murre (2021) is the ONLY published direct replication attempt. Given the study's textbook-classic status, additional replication attempts with varied environmental contrasts (open water vs pool, cold vs warm, deep vs shallow) are needed to map the parameter space in which the effect appears.

# Salamé & Baddeley (1982, 1989) and the Irrelevant Speech Effect

## The 1982 Study: Disruption of Short-Term Memory by Unattended Speech

Salamé and Baddeley's (1982) landmark paper, "Disruption of short-term memory by unattended speech: Implications for the structure of working memory" (*Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior*, 21(2), 150–164), reported a series of experiments examining the effect of unattended speech on immediate memory for visually presented digits. Key findings included:

- **Clear memory impairment**: Concurrent speech dramatically impaired memory performance even when participants were instructed to ignore it.
- **Phonological similarity matters**: The degree of impairment was a function of the *phonological similarity* between the irrelevant words and the visually presented digits—the more phonologically similar the irrelevant speech, the greater the disruption.
- **Semantics do not matter**: The semantic characteristics of the unattended speech did not influence performance; meaningful words and nonsense syllables produced equivalent disruption.
- **Articulatory suppression eliminates the effect**: Requiring subjects to suppress articulation (e.g., repeatedly saying an irrelevant word) removed the disrupting effect of irrelevant speech when material was presented visually.
- **Noise does not disrupt**: Unattended noise did not produce a reliable decrement (building on Salamé & Wittersheim, 1978).

## Theoretical Interpretation

The results were interpreted in terms of Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) working memory model, specifically the *articulatory/phonological loop*. Salamé and Baddeley suggested that verbal working memory comprises two components: a passive, phonologically based store maintained by control processes within a separate active subvocal rehearsal store. The phonological store is accessible in two ways: (1) through auditory presentation, which leads to *obligatory registration* of the material, or (2) through an *optional subvocal rehearsal process* that translates visually presented material into a phonological code. The irrelevant speech effect occurs because speech-like material gains obligatory access to the passive phonological store even when ignored, where it corrupts the memory trace of phonologically similar to-be-remembered items. Because visual material only enters the store via subvocal rehearsal, articulatory suppression (which prevents this rehearsal) eliminates the disruptive effect.

## The 1989 Study: Effects of Background Music on Phonological Short-Term Memory

Salamé and Baddeley's (1989) follow-up, "Effects of Background Music on Phonological Short-Term Memory" (*Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 41, 107–122), explored the characteristics of the exclusion process by studying the effects of music on serial recall of nine-digit sequences presented visually. Key findings:

- **Music disrupts recall**: Both vocal and instrumental music produced statistically worse serial recall than silence.
- **Speech-like stimuli are more disruptive**: Vocal music was significantly more disruptive than instrumental music; Arabic speech (unintelligible to participants) was significantly more disruptive than instrumental music. The more speech-like or digit-like the to-be-ignored stimulus, the more it interfered with digit memorization.
- **Noise remains non-disruptive**: Continuous pink noise and noise bursts did not cause significant interference compared to control conditions, all causing significantly less interference than speech-like stimuli.
- **Two proposed hypotheses**: Salamé and Baddeley (1989) developed the *Noise Filter hypothesis* (a two-stage process in which less speech-like auditory information is blocked from entering the phonological store by a filter, and then interference increases with greater phonological feature overlap) and the *Speech Detector hypothesis* (the phonological store is more sensitive to sounds sharing features with speech). They interpreted the results in terms of a phonological short-term store that excludes non-speechlike sounds.

## Legacy and Subsequent Debates

The Salamé and Baddeley studies established the *irrelevant speech effect* (also called the irrelevant sound effect): impairment of serial order memory by to-be-ignored background sound, which is specific to tasks requiring serial recall and operates on the phonological code rather than semantic content. Their "similarity of content" explanation was later challenged by Jones and Macken's (1993, 1995) *changing-state hypothesis* (the O-OER model), which argued that acoustic variability between successive irrelevant sounds—not phonological similarity to target items—determines disruption. Some later studies (e.g., LeCompte) failed to replicate the phonological similarity effect, presenting a challenge to the phonological store hypothesis. However, the Salamé and Baddeley work remains foundational for understanding auditory distraction in verbal working memory, and Baddeley himself later accepted that fluctuating/changing-state in the irrelevant stream is the crucial requirement, though he has endorsed Page and Norris's primacy model account as a good explanation of the effect.

## Kim & de Dear (2013) Study on Open-Plan Offices — Summary

The 2013 research by Jungsoo Kim and Professor Richard de Dear (University of Sydney, Faculty of Architecture and Planning) was a large-scale **re-analysis of post-occupancy survey data** from more than 42,000 office workers (one source cites 42,764 respondents). It is described as a re-analysis of a major survey dataset rather than a traditional meta-analysis. Sources differ on the geographic scope: some describe it as a U.S. survey, while The New Daily reports it covered workers in the USA, Finland, Canada, and Australia. The study was titled *"Workspace satisfaction: The privacy-communication trade off in open-plan offices."*

### Key findings on satisfaction and communication
- **Workplace satisfaction:** Workers in open-plan offices were significantly **less satisfied** with their workplace environment than those in private or cellular offices. The benefits of being close to co-workers were offset by disadvantages such as increased noise, disruption, and loss of privacy.
- **Communication:** The researchers reported their results "categorically contradict the industry-accepted wisdom that open-plan layout enhances communication between colleagues and improves occupants' overall work environmental satisfaction." In fact, satisfaction with interaction was **higher for occupants of private offices**.
- **Main sources of dissatisfaction:** Uncontrollable noise, lack of privacy/"sound privacy," and limited personal space were the primary complaints.

### Productivity
The study found many workers believed open-plan offices were **disruptive to productivity**, and the authors stated: "The open-plan proponents' argument that open-plan improves morale and productivity appears to have no basis in the research literature." The researchers concluded there is little solid evidence that open-plan layouts improve interaction between co-workers.

### Sick leave
The New Daily reports that the study found workers in open-plan offices took **62% more sick days** than those in private/cellular offices. However, it is worth noting that another source (Sourceable) attributes the 62% higher sick-leave figure to a separate 2011 study published in the *Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health* — a Danish study (Pejtersen et al.) that found average sickness absence of 8.1 days for open-plan workers versus 4.9 days for those in private offices. So there is some inconsistency across sources regarding whether the 62% sick-leave statistic comes from Kim & de Dear's 2013 study or the earlier 2011 Danish research.

**Overall conclusion of the study:** The supposed benefits of open-plan offices (better communication, collaboration, morale, and productivity) were not supported by the evidence, with open-plan workers reporting lower satisfaction and more negative workplace experiences than those in private offices.

## Summary: Mehta, Zhu & Cheema (2012) — Ambient Noise and Creativity

**The study:** In the paper *"Is Noise Always Bad? Exploring the Effects of Ambient Noise on Creative Cognition"* (Journal of Consumer Research, Vol. 39, Issue 4, December 2012, pp. 784–799, DOI: 10.1086/665048), researchers Ravi Mehta, Rui (Juliet) Zhu, and Amar Cheema conducted **five experiments** to examine how ambient noise affects creative cognition.

**Key findings on noise levels and performance:**
- A **moderate (70 dB)** level of ambient noise — roughly equivalent to a passenger car traveling on a highway — **enhanced performance on creative tasks** compared to a low (50 dB) level, and also increased the buying likelihood of innovative products.
- A **high (85 dB)** noise level — equivalent to traffic noise on a major road — **hurt creativity**.
- The relationship between noise and creativity is described as an **inverted-U curve**, with ~70 dB being the "sweet spot" (the "Goldilocks principle" — the middle is just right).

**Experimental details:** In one key experiment, 65 undergraduates completed Remote Associate Tasks (RAT) under four conditions: low noise (50 dB), moderate noise (70 dB), high noise (85 dB), and a no-noise control. The researchers used everyday multi-talker ambient noise (blended sounds from a cafeteria, roadside traffic, and distant construction) rather than white or pink noise. Results showed participants in the moderate-noise condition generated significantly more correct answers than those in the low-noise, high-noise, or control conditions.

**Mechanism:** The researchers explain that a moderate (vs. low) noise level increases processing difficulty, which induces a **higher construal level** and promotes **abstract processing** — a hallmark of creativity. Moderate noise produces just enough distraction to encourage "out-of-the-box" thinking. However, high noise creates too much distraction, which reduces the extent of information processing and thereby impairs creativity.

**Practical implication:** The authors suggest that instead of working in a quiet room, people seeking creative solutions may benefit from relatively noisy environments (e.g., a café), and marketers might consider equipping showrooms with moderate ambient noise to encourage adoption of innovative products.
